Triggers.value: A specific taste associated with the event

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that make me feel strong emotions
make sure to stay close to exit
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere
I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

issues.item: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened
issues.explanation: This item is not well aligned with the rest of the profile or the cognitive formulation. The active formulation is dominated by a Triggers–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies loop, with Negative Appraisals inactive. In contrast, punishment/self-deserving-suffering is a negative self-appraisal theme rather than a threat-management strategy, and it does not connect plausibly to the selected trigger and threat items. The other maladaptive strategies (avoiding emotional stress, staying near exits) fit the trigger-threat-hypervigilance pattern, but punishment thinking pulls toward a different clinical profile that is otherwise not represented.

vignette: Mateo was sixty-five, but the desert still lived in his chest. Twenty-eight years ago, during a routine convoy run in Iraq, an IED detonated on the road ahead. The blast hurled him against the armored bulkhead, filling the cab with acrid, coppery fumes from ruptured lines. He swallowed the bitter taste while his medic worked frantically in the dim light, and the concussion left him reeling-a persistent lightheadedness that never settled once the adrenaline finally crashed. In the years that followed, the memories refused to stay buried. Whenever a former colleague or a well-meaning stranger asked how he was, the question itself became a trigger. The moment he opened his mouth to recount the ambush, the metallic taste flooded his mouth again, and the familiar dizziness pulled at his inner ear, as if his body were still falling. As those bodily sensations surfaced in ordinary moments, Mateo's mind rewired itself to expect catastrophe. He came to believe that a sudden wave of lightheadedness was always the prelude to another attack, a physiological warning that danger was closing in. Because he constantly felt that metallic taste or that sudden spin, he immediately began scanning room peripheries and positioning himself near doorways. His nervous system shifted from memory to threat, teaching him that any unexpected noise was the opening salvo of an ambush. Because he was always plotting exits and listening for incoming fire, he could no longer tolerate situations that might unravel him emotionally. He declined staff gatherings and stepped away from deployment conversations, convinced that strong emotion would unlock panic. His hyperalertness did not fade; it sharpened his sensitivity to his own body. When his blood pressure shifted or he stood too quickly, the resulting dizziness was immediately cataloged as a danger signal rather than a simple fluctuation. His constant checking of surroundings and escape route planning kept his nervous system permanently on guard, which in turn made him hyper-sensitive to the very triggers he feared. A sharp clatter or unexpected sound was never just background noise; it was processed as an immediate threat, which in turn triggered the familiar dizziness and metallic taste. Every time he avoided a difficult conversation or positioned himself near the classroom door, his mind registered the relief but confirmed the underlying premise: the world was inherently unsafe. Over months, this pattern calcified into a rigid routine that steadily narrowed his life. The consequences of this guarded posture finally outpaced his ability to manage it alone. Teaching special education demanded a presence he no longer possessed. During a parent-teacher conference last week, a student's sudden cry sent Mateo's hand to his mouth, cutting off his words. The coppery taste coated his tongue, his vision swam, and he found himself backing toward the hallway, eyes darting to the exits. His ex-wife had tried to reach out over the years, but his insistence on controlling his environment and steering clear of heavy emotional exchanges had built a quiet wall between them. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the certainty that his mind translated ordinary sensations into survival alerts. He sought help now because the dizziness had become too frequent to ignore, and the isolation of his carefully mapped routes had left him exhausted. He hoped someone might help him relearn how to stand still in a room without counting the doors.
